rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing that the paper proposes the “first large scale benchmark and dataset, FIT-COACH, aimed at the development of video language models for situated interactions” and that “the paper addresses an interesting problem, presenting a new benchmark and methodology that have potential real-world applications.”  In the following, we address concerns --

**Data and model code:** As mentioned in Section 2 of the supplementary material, the data can be accessed at: https://developer.qualcomm.com/software/ai-datasets/qevd . We use the official code for the baseline models: InstructBLIP, Video-LLaVA, Video-ChatGPT, Video-LLaMA, LLaMA-VID and LLaVA-Next. 
Please note that the architecture of the baseline Stream-VLM model is shown in Figure 8 in the supplementary material. Furthermore, Section 5.1 of the supplementary material shows details of the vision backbone, and the special action tokens, and details of the interactive feedback generation process are shown in Section 5.4. We also provide the hyper-parameters used for training in Section 5.2 and 5.3. Please note that the baseline Stream-VLM model consists of components that are already available as open source:

Vision backbone (3D CNN): https://github.com/quic/sense \
Language backbone: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/llama2 

We will release the code along with the checkpoint for the Stream-VLM model pending internal legal review for full public release at https://github.com/Qualcomm-AI-research. We will be happy to submit the code to the reviewers during the review phase as well if there is a way to do so. 

**Evaluation Metrics -- Diversity:** Firstly, the feedbacks in the FIT-COACH benchmark have the following temporal structure: At the start of each exercise, a feedback is provided to acknowledge that the user has started, otherwise a reminder to get started is provided. A corrective feedback is provided as soon as a mistake is clearly visible. Similarly, whenever the user starts to correct their mistake, feedbacks are provided to acknowledge and guide the user to successfully correct the error. If the user is performing the exercise correctly, the feedbacks focus on repetition counting. In case repetition counts are not possible, e.g., deltoid stretches, users are provided with positive encouraging feedbacks with an average silence period of 5 seconds. Finally, at the end of each exercise a feedback focused on the overall performance during that exercise is provided. We will add these details to Section 4.2 of the supplementary material. This temporal structure ensures that feedbacks in the FIT-COACH benchmark occur at predictable time-steps, aligned to visually salient moments. Furthermore, during evaluation we consider a 3 second window around the ground-truth feedback to match with predicted feedbacks. 

Secondly, to deal with variability in the feedbacks themselves, we use a mix of four metrics: METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERT and LLM-Acc (c.f. Section 5.1 in the main paper). The METEOR, ROUGE-L ensures that the predicted feedbacks match at a word level to the ground-truth feedbacks: e.g., in case of a corrective feedback where the person is not moving their arms, the METEOR, ROUGE-L terms ensure that the predicted feedback refers to the “arm” and “not moving” terms. The BERT score and the LLM-Acc metric on the other hand matches feedbacks at a semantic level. Thus, the chosen combination of metrics ensures that the predicted feedbacks match the ground-truth both at the semantic level while containing references to specific terms, e.g., “arm” and “not moving”, as required. We will clarify in the final version, thank you. 

**Evaluation Metrics – LLM evaluation:** Thanks for the comment. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of LLM evaluation (LLM-Acc metric in Tables 3,4 of the main paper), we conduct a human evaluation where we ask users to rate the responses. The human evaluation is conducted on a smaller set of 200 feedbacks from the FIT-COACH benchmark.  We add the results to Table 2 of the attached rebuttal pdf (for the best performing fine-tuned models (see also Table 4 in the main paper). Furthermore, we use two additional LLMs: LLaMA-3-8b-Instruct and LLaMA-3-70b-Instruct to score the feedbacks, using the same prompt as for Mixtral- Instruct-0.1  as in Tables 3 and 4 of the main paper. We find remarkable agreement between the LLMs and the human evaluators, especially with respect to the relative ranking of the models by performance. We will add these results to the main paper.

| Evaluation Model | Socratic-Llama-2-7B | Video-ChatGPT fine-tuned  | Stream-VLM | Stream-VLM (w/o 3D CNN) | Stream-VLM (w/o Action-Tokens) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Human | 2.63 | 2.59 | **2.80** | 2.51 | 2.71 |
| Mixtral-Instruct-0.1  | 2.39 | 2.42 | **2.56** | 2.17 | 2.56 |
| LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct | 1.74 | 1.82 | **1.90** | 1.62 | 1.89 |
| LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct | 2.17 | 2.33 | **2.45** | 2.11 | 2.41 |

**Construction of the dataset:** We have provided details of the FIT-COACH benchmark in Section 3.1 of the main paper and Section 4.2 of the supplementary materials. We provide details of the data collection setup and the instructions provided to the participants. Additionally, we will expand upon the description in Section 4.2 of the supplementary materials, focusing on additional details of the annotation process. Thank you for the suggestion.

We also provide details of the FIT-COACH dataset in Section 3.2 of the main paper. We provide details of the collection and annotation process of the fine-grained short videos in Section 4.1 of the supplementary materials, including web interface used in the collection process in Figure 7. We also describe the generation process for the fitness questions in the FIT-COACH dataset in Section 4.1. The long-range videos in the FIT-COACH dataset are collected using the same process as the videos in the FIT-COACH benchmark.

We thank the reviewer for recognizing that the FIT-COACH benchmark and dataset “would be greatly helpful for future development of fitness materials” and that the “paper is well organized, with proper examples and composition including dataset and models newly proposed.” In the following, we address concerns --

**Title can mislead readers:** We would be happy to update the title to “Live Fitness Coaching as a Testbed for Situated Interaction” to enhance the focus on the fitness setup.

**Background scene:** The main goal of the FIT-COACH benchmark is to produce the correct feedback at the right time. This depends on correctly recognizing movements of the participants including mistakes. As the focus is on the movements of the participants, we keep the set of participants in the train/val sets and the test set disjoint. The background scenes in FIT-COACH mimic real-world fitness coaching setups and are highly varied, as shown in Figures 1,2 and 3, as well as the videos in the supplementary material. The diversity in the backgrounds is ensured by the data collection process, which involves crowdworkers recoding videos in locations of their choosing. Thus, we do not expect significant bias in the training or inference caused by the background. We will clarify in the final version, thank you.

**License terms:**  The dataset is released with a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license, which permits dataset use and sharing with appropriate attribution. Please note that these details are provided in Section 2 of the supplementary materials and in the dataset webpage: https://developer.qualcomm.com/software/ai-datasets/qevd (see section titled “Dataset license”).

We thank the reviewer for recognizing that the “benchmark and the dataset is novel in terms of its purpose -- situated interaction, and may be beneficial to the community”. We also thank the reviewer for recognizing that the baseline Stream-VLM model “outperforms other existing video language models, namely LLaMA-VID, showing its effectiveness”. In the following, we address the concerns --

**Prior Work (Kim et al., FixMyPose: Pose Correctional Captioning and Retrieval, AAAI 2021):** We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important prior work and we will update the main paper to discuss the same.

**Domain of the dataset:** While the domain of the dataset is limited to fitness coaching, it has real-world applications (lines 43-44) as home workouts are growing rapidly in popularity as confirmed by multiple surveys (https://www.statista.com/topics/12564/home-fitness/#topicOverview). An interactive fitness coaching model can thus bring real-world benefits to people. Furthermore, as mentioned in lines 35-44, this real-world scenario has several benefits that make it an ideal test-bed for studying situated dialogue: it has a relatively controlled structure and it is a highly challenging unsolved problem for current AI systems. We will clarify this, thank you for the suggestion.

**Novelty of baseline model:** As noted in Section 4 (titled “Baseline Stream-VLM”) and lines 51-55 of Section 1 (Introduction), we emphasize that the proposed model is a baseline for interactive feedback generation. While the 3D CNN is indeed an important component for the success of the model, unlike state-of-the- art vision-language models, e.g., LLaMA-VID or LLaVA-Next, it is interactive and not limited to “turn-based” interactions. The baseline model is designed to be a possible starting point for future work that generates interactive feedbacks on our FIT-COACH benchmark.

**Quality of dataset:** The quality of the dataset annotations were rigorously verified as described below: 
-  Long-range videos: The annotated feedbacks of every video were verified by a second annotator before release. We include example videos in the supplementary material to demonstrate the overall quality of annotations. The full dataset can be accessed at: https://developer.qualcomm.com/software/ai-datasets/qevd

- Short-clip fine-grained labels: Each video and corresponding annotation was manually reviewed for correctness by at least one unique crowd-worker. 

We will clarify this in the final version. Furthermore, we include an ablation in Table 1 of the attached rebuttal pdf, where the baseline Stream-VLM model is not pre-trained on the fitness questions and feedbacks of the short-clips. We see a significant decrease in performance, highlighting  the effectiveness of the fitness questions and feedbacks of the short-clips pairs for the development of interactive models for fitness coaching.

**Model section details:** Please note that the architecture of the baseline Stream-VLM model is shown in Figure 8 in the supplementary material. Furthermore, Section 5.1 of the supplementary material shows details of the vision backbone, and the special action tokens, and details of the interactive feedback generation process are shown in Section 5.4. We also provide the hyper-parameters used for training in Section 5.2 and 5.3. We will update Section 4 in the main paper to point the readers to the specific sections in the supplementary material. Thank you for the suggestion.

**QA pairs:** Please note that the details of the generation process, including that of the prompts used, can be found in Section 4.1 of the supplementary materials. As discussed there, the QA pairs were generated using the Mixtral-8B-Instruct model. The question generation process follows the scheme detailed in “Visual Instruction Tuning, NeurIPS 2023 (Oral)”. In Table 1 of the attached rebuttal pdf, where the baseline Stream-VLM model is not pre-trained on the QA pairs and feedbacks of the short-clips. We see a significant decrease in performance, highlighting  the effectiveness of the QA pairs for the development of interactive models for fitness coaching. We will update main paper to clarify this, thank you for the suggestion.

**Long vs. Short video feedbacks:** As described in L144-145 of the main paper, the short video feedbacks occur at the end of each short video clip. This is in contrast to the feedbacks on the long-range videos, which can occur at any time within the video clip. We provide additional details of feedbacks on the short video clips in Section 4.1 of the supplementary material. We will clarify in the final version, thank you for the suggestion.

**Pre-trained adapter weights:** We fine-tune the adapter weights as current state-of-the-art models, e.g., LLaMA-VID or LLaVA-Next, cannot recognize fine-grained human actions (c.f., Table 3 and Section 5.2 of the main paper). Recognizing fine-grained human actions, e.g. mistakes during  a fitness routine, is the key to success in the FIT-COACH benchmark. The use of pre-trained adapter weights is an interesting direction of future research.

**Typo**: We will correct the typo (“supplemental” -> “supplementary materials”). Thank you.

We thank the reviewer for the review and acknowledging that current “VLMs are not sufficiently robust for situated interaction cases” and that “this paper is inspiring a new domain where VLMs have to be further tuned.” In the following, we address the concerns --

**Lab environment:** The long-range videos were recorded in a lab environment due to the constrains imposed by the recording setup. Regarding the motions of the participants, as noted in L105-107, although the participants were instructed to perform mistakes of the exercises shown on the screen, they were not required to follow the motion exactly as shown. This leads to natural variations in motion as evidenced by the videos in the supplementary materials. This recording setup in FIT-COACH is also crucial to capture a wide range of possible mistakes, which is an essential component of a representative benchmark such as FIT-COACH. The short-clips in the FIT-COACH dataset on the other hand involves crowdworkers recoding videos in diverse locations of their choosing, e.g., homes. We will clarify in the final version, thank you.

summary_and_contributions.value: VLMs are not sufficiently robust for situated interaction cases. As one of such challenging scenarios, the authors proposed the FIT-COACH benchmark that explores human-AI interaction in the real-world fitness coaching domain. Experimental results showed that conventional VLMs are not sufficient to tackle such interaction cases and authors proposed a simple baseline VLMs that are tuned to work well for the task.

review.value:
(+) Good motivation and good result obtained.
(+) Dataset has sufficient difference to conventional action recognition domain and also proposed algorithm significantly beats conventional VLMs.
(+) Experiments are thorough enough.
(-) The dataset is simulated in the lab rather than collected in the real-world gym environment.

strengths.value:
The dataset setting seems practical and also representative for situated interaction cases.

Compared to conventional action recognition benchmark, the proposed benchmark has enough difference: it has text annotations for coaching and this seems useful and hard to collect. Also, the entire dataset scale is large.

The scenario tackled is sufficiently different from what conventional VLMs are good at and this paper is inspiring a new domain where VLMs have to be further tuned.

The new baseline is obtained and it significantly outperforms conventional VLMs in the desired application.

The experiments are informative and included recent competitive VLMs.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: One of the weaknesses of this dataset is that it is recorded inside the lab environment rather than in the gym environment. Also, most of motions are simulated rather than captured for realistic behaviors. These weaken the reality of the dataset; while avoiding this might be technically non-trivial.

limitations.value: Limitation is discussed in the conclusion.

clarity.value: The paper is well written and well presented.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper is well positioned. It has sufficient difference to previous VLMs and also action recognition benchmarks.

title.value: New fitness coaching dataset and baseline model for situated interaction

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes a new benchmark dataset of fitness coaching videos with question-answering and feedback annotations for situated interaction, which is novel in terms of its purpose (situated interaction) even though its domain is limited to fitness coaching. In addition, the authors conduct experiments: 1) comparison of state-of-the-art video-language models on the proposed benchmark dataset, showing its inferior performances compared to the fine-tuned model, and 2) comparison of fine-tuned models with the proposed model, demonstrating its efficacy.

review.value:
Pros:
- Writing is easy to follow.
- The proposed benchmark dataset is novel in terms of its purpose -- situated interaction, and may be beneficial to the community.
- The proposed model outperforms other existing video language models, namely LLaMA-VID, showing its effectiveness.

Cons:
- The domain of the dataset is only about fitness coaching, which limits its usefulness in real-world applications.
- The proposed model is not novel, and its effectiveness may come from using 3D CNN instead of ViT as backed by the reported result (STREAM-VLM (w/o 3D CNN) performs worse than LLaMA-VID in Table 4).
- The quality of dataset was not verified. It would be desirable to do experiments to confirm its quality such as annotations.
- Even though writing is easy to follow in general, it lacks details. e.g., the model section may need more detail and model figure to help understanding. In addition, it also lacks some details regarding the data collection process (see below).

strengths.value:
- Writing is easy to follow.
- The proposed benchmark dataset is novel in terms of its purpose -- situated interaction, and may be beneficial to the community.
- The proposed model outperforms other existing video language models, namely LLaMA-VID, showing its effectiveness.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposes FIT-Coach benchmark that aims to assess human-AI interaction in real-world fitness coaching, which requires monitoring user activity and providing feedback, considering the real-time and timeliness. The dataset consists of long-range videos with live feedbacks (including corrective ones) evaluated with SOTA VLMs including Stream-VLM authors newly propose.

review.value: Overall paper is well organized, with proper examples and composition including dataset and models newly proposed.

strengths.value: This paper deals with live and corrective feedback video for fitness, the area which had been investigated with less consideration on multimodal annotations. Authors construct a dataset that consists of videos of sufficient play hours, covering the area of long-range, interactive, mistakes and corrective feedbacks. It is believed that the dataset format would be greatly helpful for future development of fitness materials, considering that crowdworker-based collection of data would improve the generalizability of the applicability of the fitness contents. The paper fairly introduces their contribution as dataset construction and the model development that follows.

title.value: What to Say and When to Say it: Live Fitness Coaching as a Testbed for Situated Interaction

summary_and_contributions.value:
- This paper proposes the first large scale benchmark and dataset, FIT-COACH, aimed at the development of video language models for situated interactions.  The chosen scenario for this benchmark is live fitness coaching, where an AI model interacts with a user through language while viewing the user in real-time via a camera. 
- They perform an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art VLMs on this task, which shows that the task is a largely unsolved with significant room for improvement.
- The authors propose a novel video language model, STREAM-VLM, which moves beyond turn-based interactions.

review.value:
The quality of this paper is commendable. It is well-written, clearly described, and logically organized, making it easy to follow and understand. The paper addresses an interesting problem, presenting a new benchmark and methodology that have potential real-world applications.

### Pros
- The paper addresses a highly interesting and relevant research problem. By focusing on real-time interaction between the model and users, it aims to enhance user learning and support, particularly in the context of live fitness coaching.
- The experimental analysis is thorough, with the authors testing a wide range of baseline models. This extensive evaluation helps to underscore the effectiveness and limitations of the proposed method.

### Cons
- One significant drawback is the absence of provided data and model code. This omission makes it challenging to verify the dataset's usability and reproduce the results, which is crucial for the scientific community to build upon this work.

In summary, the paper presents a high-quality and impactful contribution to the field, addressing a novel and meaningful problem. However, the availability of data and code would greatly enhance the reproducibility and practical applicability of the research.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
While the paper presents a significant and impactful contribution, there are some areas where improvements can be made:

### Evaluation Metrics
- Concerns About Evaluation Metrics: I have some concerns regarding the evaluation metrics used for this task. Given the nature of the task, models may generate diverse responses at different time points. This variability can make it challenging to consistently evaluate model performance.
- Use of Language Models for Evaluation: The paper mentions using LM to evaluate results. While this can be an efficient method, it raises questions about the accuracy and reliability of the evaluation. Language models may introduce biases or errors, potentially affecting the perceived performance of the proposed method.

correctness.value:
The claims made in the submission are generally correct. However, the construction of the dataset is not particularly clear. More detailed information on the data collection and organization would improve transparency.

The evaluation methods and experiment design are appropriate and well-executed, with a comprehensive set of baseline models tested.

documentation.value: The submission does not provide access to the dataset and benchmarks, which raises concerns about responsible use and reproducibility.

title.value: What to Say and When to Say it: Live Fitness Coaching as a Testbed for Situated Interaction

abstract.value: Vision-language models have shown impressive progress in recent years. However, existing models are largely limited to turn-based interactions, where each turn must be stepped (i.e., prompted) by the user. Open-ended, asynchronous interactions, where an AI model may proactively deliver timely responses or feedback based on the unfolding situation in real-time, are an open challenge. In this work, we present the QEVD benchmark and dataset, which explores human-AI interaction in the challenging, yet controlled, real-world domain of fitness coaching – a task which intrinsically requires monitoring live user activity and providing immediate feedback. The benchmark requires vision-language models to recognize complex human actions, identify possible mistakes, and provide appropriate feedback in real-time. Our experiments reveal the limitations of existing state-of-the-art vision-language models for such asynchronous situated interactions. Motivated by this, we propose a simple end-to-end streaming baseline that can respond asynchronously to human actions with appropriate feedback at the appropriate time.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')

Reviewers are expected to have at least two papers in top peer-reviewed conferences or journals, with at least one paper in a machine learning venue (e.g., NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR) in the last three years, though we still ask that you nominate one of the authors even if none meet this requirement. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.
